prerequisites: Prior knowledge in Physical Fundamentals of Engineering
Prior knowledge in Calculus and Algebra

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge of the principles of theory of machines and mechanisms.
Knowledge and use of the principles of strength of materials.
Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, that enables them to learn new methods and theories, and provides them with versatility to adapt to new situations.

Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, critical reasoning and to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills and abilities in the field of Industrial Engineering, specific mechanical technology.
Adopt a responsible, orderly attitude to work and be willing to learn, considering the challenge that continuous training will pose.

Apply the strategies of scientific methodology: analyze the problematic situation qualitatively and quantitatively, propose hypotheses and solutions using the models of industrial engineering, Mechanical specialty.
Work effectively in a group, integrating capacities and knowledge to make decisions in the field of industrial engineering, Mechanical specialty.

Know, understand and apply the basic concepts and principles of strength of materials and of mechanisms and machines that enable students for the subsequent learning of advanced methods and theories of mechanical engineering.

Appropriately apply the strategies of scientific methodology to the problems posed by mechanical systems: qualitatively and quantitatively analyze the situation, propose hypotheses and solutions using the models of applied mechanics.

Adequately express theoretical knowledge, resolution methods and results inherent to the problems posed by the equilibrium and movement of solids and mechanical systems, using specific vocabulary and terminology.
Work effectively in a group, integrating capacities and knowledge to formulate ideas, debate proposals and make decisions in the development of works typical of applied mechanics.
Adopt a responsible, orderly attitude to work and be willing to learn, demonstrating critical spirit and interest in aspects related to the subject.
Ability to independently tackle the modeling of a mechanical system composed of rigid solids and simple mechanical elements.
Ability to evaluate how loads are transmitted to supports in simple isostatic structures.
Ability for kinematic analysis, obtaining velocities and accelerations, at points and elements, in reference to absolute or relative systems, of simple mechanisms.
Ability to deduce centers of gravity and inertia properties of solids and elementary flat areas.
Ability for dynamic analysis of simple mechanisms, both planar and spatial.
Ability to evaluate the variation of internal forces in simple beams under point or distributed loads.
Ability to evaluate stresses in simple elements.
Ability to transmit these results understandably to a specialized audience.

syllabus_topics: Topic 1: Systems of forces
Basic notions and operations of vector calculus
Definition and properties of moment of a force with respect to a point and an axis
Concept and properties of a couple of forces
Equivalence and reduction of systems of forces
Topic 2: Centroids
Concept and properties of center of gravity
Static moment
Determination of centroids of elementary figures
Pappus-Guldinus theorems
Topic 3: Static equilibrium
Study of structural systems, fundamental axiom of static equilibrium of the rigid solid
Concepts of connection and mechanical action of connection
Calculation of the stresses acting on each of the elements into which a mechanical system can be decomposed
Analysis of isostatic structures and calculation methods for trusses
Topic 4: Friction
Study of Coulomb's simplified hypothesis for the analysis of sliding friction, friction coefficients and friction angle
Industrial applications of friction, self-retention
Topic 5: Cables
Study of the equilibrium of funicular solids, cables subjected to discrete and continuous forces
Parabolic cable
Analysis of catenaries
Topic 6: Kinematics of the rigid solid
Concepts of particle velocity and acceleration
Analysis of simple translational and rotational movements of the rigid solid
Meaning of angular velocity and acceleration vectors
Derivation law in moving bases
Velocity and acceleration fields
Study of the relative motion of a point and a solid with respect to a moving system
Topic 7: Kinematics of planar motion
Particularities of planar motion
Concepts of instantaneous center of rotation and succession velocity
Concept of base and roulette
Geometry of planar motion, graphical calculation of velocities
Study of accelerations in planar rolling motion
Pole of accelerations and notable circles
Topic 8: Inertia properties of solids
Moments of inertia with respect to axes, planes and points
Products of inertia
Steiner's theorems
Elementary figures
Inertia tensor and obtaining the principal directions of inertia of a solid
Topic 9: Dynamics of the rigid solid
Fundamental dynamic magnitudes of dynamics, momentum and angular momentum
Fundamental theorems of dynamics
Expressions for angular momentum and kinetic energy in rigid solids
Concept of inertial force and gyroscopic couple
Application of D'Alembert's Principle to the dynamic analysis of mechanisms
Topic 10: Dynamics of the solid with fixed axis
Study of solids with rotational motion around a fixed axis
Obtaining reactions at supports
Rotor balancing
Topic 11: Planar dynamics
Particularization of dynamic magnitudes and equations to planar motion
Presentation of different types of dynamic problems and how to solve them
Application to mechanical systems that make up machines and mechanisms
Topic 12: Moments of inertia of area
Description of moments and products of inertia of planar areas
Principal moments of inertia and principal directions using Mohr's circle
Topic 13: Internal forces
Concept of internal force on a section of a solid
Axial, shear and bending forces
Representation of force diagrams along straight axis elements
Topic 14: Normal stresses
Concept of normal stress and longitudinal unit deformation
Relationship between stress and deformation in uniaxial states, Hooke's Law
Relationship between stresses and section forces
Normal stresses due to axial force and bending moment in a principal plane of inertia
teaching_methods: Seminars (problem solving, some in computer labs)
assessment_rules: For the ordinary call, evaluation is mixed, combining continuous assessment tasks (20%) and exams (80%). The first partial exam (covering topics 1-7) requires a minimum score of 5/10 to clear the material. Students who pass the first partial will have their final exam grade calculated as the geometric mean of both partials; those who do not pass or take the first partial must take a comprehensive final exam. Alternatively, students can opt for a single final exam constituting 100% of the grade, by notifying the faculty before week 4 of the second semester. All exams weigh theory at 40% and problems at 60%. Failure to take the second partial or the final exam results in a 'Not presented' grade for the entire course, and ethical violations lead to a 0.0 grade. For the extraordinary call, students take a single comprehensive exam. By default, 20% from course tasks is maintained, with the exam being 80% of the final grade. If the 100% exam score is higher, that score will be considered for the final grade. Failure to take the extraordinary exam results in a 'Not presented' grade.
